title: Strengthening dual bounds for multicommodity capacitated network design with unsplittable flow constraints
contribution: For path-based unsplittable multicommodity capacitated network design, a multiple-choice binary capacity reformulation, a proof that the single-arc relaxation hull has the form Gx <= Hy with nonnegative G, H and no constant, two new cover-type cut families (SAC-Pack, Gen-SAC-Pack) with exact separation, and an integrated scheme with Lagrangian-selected helper metric inequalities that strengthens commercial-solver dual bounds on industrial e-commerce instances and the Canad set.
problem_entry: Fulfilment networks require one path per commodity, forcing binary flows; primal heuristics exist but solution quality cannot be assessed because LP-based dual bounds are weak, so the paper targets dual bounds (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Binarize integer capacities into a multiple-choice selector, characterize the sign/homogeneous form of the single-arc hull, derive packing-count cuts (alpha_t = commodities that fit in t units) and bounded-coefficient generalizations, and add redundant helper metric inequalities chosen by a Lagrangian LP re-solve (pp. 5-19).
assumptions: Pre-given path sets, single facility type in integer multiples, no pre-existing capacity and one capacity level per arc (named as what makes the hull homogeneous with nonnegative coefficients), integer data in the arc set S (pp. 3-9).
proof_devices: disjunctive extended formulation of S = (0,0) U (S^t, e_t) plus Fourier-Motzkin projection with zero right-hand sides gives a homogeneous description (Prop. 1, p. 8)
zeroing-out argument: a negative x-coefficient can be replaced by 0 to get a dominating valid inequality, so G >= 0; points (0, e_p) give H >= 0 (pp. 8-9)
validity of SAC-Pack by restriction to Z and a cardinality-constrained knapsack definition of alpha_t (Prop. 2, p. 10)
exact separation IP with precedence constraints on non-decreasing demands (model (11), pp. 11-13)
Boyd-style row generation between a cut LP and a feasibility oracle for Gen-SAC-Pack (pp. 14-15)
bounded-coefficient knapsack solved by min-knapsack DP over objective values plus bisection, O(n^2 B log(nB)) (App. B, pp. 28-29)
two-commodity example showing BIN linking constraints beat INT ones (App. A, pp. 27-28)
experiments: Python 3.10, Gurobi 11.0, 24-core Xeon; 15 synthetic path-based instances from a U.S. e-commerce company's data (3 groups) and 31 Canad arc-based instances; INT vs BIN (gap improvement 38.5/12.4/2.6%), LP strengthening vs disaggregated linking and r-split c-strong (79.8% on Group 1, 85.3% vs 82.7% on Canad), ICG solves 4/5 Group 1 and beats 12 h plain BIN by 26.5% and 22.5% on Groups 2-3 with generation time inside the 3 h budget, helper-inequality check under Gurobi/CPLEX/SCIP (pp. 20-27, 30).
positioning: Extends the arc-set polyhedron line (c-strong, r-split c-strong, Min-Set, Chen et al. 2021); difference from Chen et al. stated as model assumptions (no constant term); bound comparison with Hewitt et al. branch-and-price flagged as somewhat unfair (pp. 3-4, 9, 25-26).
writing: Four contribution bullets on p. 2; weak LP root cause shown in one step-vs-linear cost figure; each cut family introduced with a numerical LP point it cuts off; results quantified paragraph by paragraph with explicit hedges where comparisons favour the authors (pp. 2, 6-7, 10-14, 22-26).
limits_future: BIN alone still leaves small instances unsolved; Gen-SAC-Pack not worth its time on Canad; helper inequalities take about 1.5 h on Group 3; no explanation of why redundant metric inequalities help; future work only generic integration into other bounding schemes (pp. 6, 16, 25, 27, 30).

transferable: Binarize an integer capacity into a multiple-choice selector so each capacity level gets its own knapsack and level-specific cut coefficients (pp. 5, 8-10).

title: Geoffrion's theorem beyond finiteness and rationality
contribution: Shows by two explicit irrational-polyhedron examples that Geoffrion's theorem (Lagrangian dual value equals the convexified primal) can fail for both conv(X) and its closure, and proves it holds when conv(X) is locally polyhedral with an attained optimum, when n <= 2, or when the dualized system is a single rational row.
problem_entry: Geoffrion's theorem is proved only for finite X or integer points of rational polyhedra because the proof needs conv(X) polyhedral; only a sentence by Guignard flags the gap (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Counterexamples first (v^L < v* and v^L < closed v*), diagnose them as boundary-of-hull degeneracies, dispose of the interior case by Slater, then prove three sufficient conditions for the boundary case (pp. 2-5).
assumptions: Minimization IP with X a subset of Z^n and dualized Ax >= b; Thm 1.2 needs local polyhedrality and attainment of the closed-hull problem (called crucial), Thm 1.3 n <= 2, Thm 1.4 a rational single row and finite inf over X (pp. 1, 5, 7).
proof_devices: weak-duality ordering v^L <= closed v* <= v* (Prop. 2.1, p. 6)
Slater's condition for the relative-interior case (Prop. 1.1, pp. 5-6)
box localization around the optimum plus Farkas; box facets inactive at an interior point so active hull inequalities are globally valid (Thm 1.2, p. 6)
extreme-point counting in three types to show planar hulls are locally polyhedral (Lemma 2.2, pp. 6-7)
three-case split on how X meets integer hyperplanes a.x = beta with b - a.x >= 1 off the hyperplane and large lambda (Thm 1.4, p. 7)
recession-cone equality and Rockafellar Cor. 9.8.1 to compute a closed hull in the counterexample (pp. 4-5)
example with only an irrational separating hyperplane to show the natural proof route fails for multi-row systems (Ex. 3.1, p. 8)
positioning: Extends Geoffrion 1974 without correcting it; answers an unproved remark of Guignard 1998; tools from Dey-Moran 2013 and textbook convex analysis; future link to De Loera et al. 2025 on finitely generated integer points (pp. 1-2, 4-8).
writing: Theorem stated, two worked counterexamples with figures, then three announced results in the introduction; standard facts proved 'for the sake of completeness'; careful about which equality holds under which theorem (pp. 1-6).
limits_future: Open: Thm 1.2 without attainment, Thm 1.4 for rational multi-row systems (with an example why the obvious proof fails), connections to Hilbert-basis finiteness under group actions (pp. 7-8).

method_links.note: counterexample for the dropped hypothesis, sufficient conditions, lemma shown to fail in R^3, open cases with the key assumption named
studies when a Lagrangian dual bound equals the convexified primal, i.e. certificate quality, at the level of theory

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: test a classical theorem's implicit hypothesis by counterexample, then give sufficient conditions
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Geoffrion's theorem's finiteness/rationality hypothesis is dropped, two counterexamples given, three sufficient conditions proved

transferable: Compare the dual value with both the hull and the closed-hull primal; a counterexample may break one equality and not the other (pp. 2-3, 5).
Use Slater to dispose of the interior case and reduce a duality question to the boundary of conv(X) (p. 5).
Localize to a box where a convex set is a polytope, apply LP duality, and show box constraints carry no multiplier (p. 6).
State each open case with the natural proof strategy and an example where that strategy fails though the conclusion holds (p. 8).
coauthors: Frederic Meunier, Diego A. Moran R.

quotes.text: The challenge for extending Geoffrion’s theorem beyond finiteness and rationality is thus to understand integer programs whose feasibility set lies on the boundary of conv(X).
We note here that (3) having an optimal solution is a crucial assumption in our proof.

title: Decomposition of Sparse Integer Programs via Nonlinear Edge Encodings and Column-and-Row Generation
contribution: Turns the zero-gap decomposable Lagrangian dual of Cifuentes-Dey-Xu into an exact, decomposable, structurally general column-and-row generation algorithm for tree-structured binary programs, proves exponential separations among Vertex, Monomial, Reflected and Generalized encoding families (and that Generalized is not universal), and shows computationally that CRG beats a monolithic solve while richer encodings perform worse.
problem_entry: Dual decomposition is parallel but leaves a gap; their own IPCO 2025 zero-gap dual needs exponentially many redundant nonlinear consistency constraints and subgradient methods give no primal point to separate from, so 'a zero-gap Lagrangian dual is not yet an algorithm' (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Solve the Geoffrion-style primal characterization by Dantzig-Wolfe: price lifted local integer columns per block in parallel and separate violated encoding rows from the difference of boundary distributions on each edge; the encoding family enters only through a separation oracle (pp. 3, 6-9).
assumptions: Block interaction graph is a tree, shared variables binary, local sets otherwise arbitrary; exactness requires a complete family and exact separation; separation of set-based encodings is a MIP; experiments with 15 blocks of 100 binaries, q in {20,30,40}, four topologies, 5 seeds (pp. 3, 5, 8-11, 20-21).
proof_devices: inclusion-exclusion: Monomial and Reflected span the same function space, giving exactness of Reflected and Generalized (Lemma 4.1, Cor. 4.2-4.3, p. 11)
gadget lemma: on a one-edge F/complement instance, k rows close the gap iff a margin separator with k family terms exists, proved from master duals and reduced costs (Lemma 5.9, pp. 13-14)
complementation symmetry z -> 1-z swapping Monomial and Reflected to transfer bounds (p. 14)
Minsky-Papert polynomial threshold degree of group covering and parity (Thms 5.10, 5.12, pp. 15, 17)
random restrictions with a binomial tail bound killing high-degree terms while keeping n/4 free variables (Lemma 5.11, Lemma 5.13, pp. 14-18)
four-point affine identity on disjoint quadruples for the 2^(n/3) Vertex lower bound (Thm 5.5, p. 17)
single parity encoding closing a gap that needs exponentially many Generalized rows (Thm 5.6, Prop. 5.7, pp. 13, 18-19)
experiments: Python 3.13, Gurobi 13.0.1, EC2 16 vCPU, 1800 s; 180 stable-set and dominating-set instances over star/path/binary/random trees; lexicographic ranking (solved, censored time, gap) fixed in advance; CRG variants beat monolithic (stable set Hybrid 50/90 vs 14/90; dominating set Vertex 19/90 vs 0/90); topology/coupling/stochastic breakdown; integer L-shaped and scenario decomposition faster on star instances; row-diversity statistics (budget share, density, Jaccard, near duplicates) explain why Reflected/Generalized underperform (pp. 21-31).
positioning: Related work placed on three axes (exactness, decomposability, structural generality): Lagrangian/progressive hedging inexact, L-shaped/Benders/SDDiP need master-recourse structure, augmented and semi-Lagrangian lose decomposability, nonserial DP and Bienstock-Munoz LPs need exponential objects; Benders-type credited as closest in spirit; scope claim is a common mechanism, not a replacement for specialized methods (pp. 4-5, 32).
writing: Bold argumentative paragraph heads, four numbered contributions, all separation theorems stated before proofs, and the headline computational lesson stated against the theory (pp. 2-4, 12-13, 32).
limits_future: Specialized methods faster on stars; interface size drives difficulty; Generalized family not universal; future work on adaptive encoding selection and problem-specific encodings; Remark 5.8 modelling rule to expose cross-block implications locally (pp. 13, 27-28, 32).

title: Branching with a pre-specified finite list of k-sparse split sets for binary MILPs
contribution: For branching on k-sparse split disjunctions in binary MILPs, shows that the {-1,0,1} list dominates all 2-sparse splits, that no finite list suffices for k >= 3, that any finite list has covering number at least floor(k/2), and that the {-1,0,1} list has covering number at most k-1 for k <= 4, justifying such lists for low sparsity.
problem_entry: Several computational papers obtain much smaller trees by branching on fixed-sparsity disjunctions with coefficients in {-1,0,1}, a pre-specified finite list, without theoretical justification (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Dominance of split sets on the unit cube (cannot increase tree size) and a covering number (tree grows by at most 2^(p-1)) as geometric proxies; positive at k=2, impossibility at k>=3, lower and upper bounds on covering numbers (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Pure binary MILPs, integer split disjunctions with ||pi||_0 <= k, dominance measured on [0,1]^n independent of the LP; tree-size consequences are worst-case factors, not measured (pp. 1-3).
proof_devices: WLOG sorting 0 <= pi_1 <= ... <= pi_k by complementing and permuting variables, valid because F_k is closed under these operations (p. 4)
exhaustive case analysis on eta versus partial sums of pi, k = 3, 4 reduced to k-1 by conditioning on x_k (pp. 4, 6-8)
infinite family S_gamma whose dominating split is pinned by boundary cube vertices and fails as gamma grows (Thm 2, pp. 4-5)

pigeonhole to fix p <= k-1 sets for infinitely many targets, then a nonzero solution of k+p < 2k homogeneous equations moves a cube vertex into S^theta inside one arrangement cell (Lemma 1, Thm 3, pp. 5-6)
positioning: Sides with the dense-branching computational literature against the 1-sparse default while citing his own random-instance result for 1-sparse branching; uses finiteness of split closures for cutting planes as the contrasting foil (pp. 1-3).
writing: Short-note format with main results and conclusions before proofs; each negative result followed by 'the next natural question'; the k = 3 lower bound of 2 in the conclusions rests on Thm 2 rather than Thm 3's floor(k/2) (my reading) (pp. 2-4).
limits_future: Open whether F_k is optimal for larger k; Thm 3 and Prop. 4 may need tightening; only k=3 of Thm 2 and the even case of Thm 3 proved in full; result read as a warning that problem-specific dense disjunctions may be needed (pp. 3-6).

method_links.note: an empirically successful branching practice shrunk to a geometric proxy with a measure defined for every split, followed by how much of the practice it justifies and where it points elsewhere
positive k=2 result, impossibility for k>=3, lower bound floor(k/2) vs upper bound k-1 with the gap stated as open

transferable: Define a dominance relation that provably cannot increase tree size and a covering number with an explicit tree-size factor, so a geometric quantity has algorithmic meaning (pp. 2-3).
Cut case analysis by symmetry after checking the candidate list is closed under the same symmetries (p. 4).
Prove that no finite list works by a one-parameter family of targets, pigeonhole on finitely many candidates and a dimension count (pp. 5-6).
Write conclusions as both a justification of a practice and a warning about its ceiling (pp. 3-4).

quotes.text: If one can show that a finite list of k-sparse disjunctions has a small covering number, then it could be considered a theoretical justification for using just this finite list of pre-specified k-sparse disjunctions instead of general k-sparse disjunctions.
More generally, Theorem 3 may also be an indication that the use of pre-specified list of disjunctions may not be the best way to generate small branch-and-bound trees.

title: Copositive Matrices with Ordered Off-Diagonal Entries
contribution: Proves that copositive matrices whose off-diagonal entries are nondecreasing in rows and columns (and relaxed and block variants, and their scaling/permutation orbit) are SPN, gives polynomial membership tests, and derives exactness of the DNN/SPN relaxation for new classes of standard quadratic programs, resolving the Dey-Kocuk conjecture that separable StQPs have tight DNN relaxations.
problem_entry: Classical question of when copositive implies SPN (equal only for n <= 4), triggered by an open conjecture from Dey-Kocuk 2025 that the DNN relaxation of separable standard quadratic programs is always tight (pp. 1-2, 13).
key_idea: An induction framework via row deletion and Schur complements (one-sign row, closure under deletion and Schur complement), shown to hold for ordered off-diagonal matrices; since this class is invariant under adding multiples of the all-ones matrix, SPN and COP bounds coincide for StQP, and separable objectives permute into the class (pp. 4-6, 11-13).
assumptions: Symmetric real matrices; StQP over the simplex with CP/COP reformulation and DNN/SPN relaxation, strong duality in both pairs; general framework condition (3.1.III) recursive and hard to check, hence concrete ordered classes (pp. 4-5, 11).
proof_devices: induction on n from Diananda's n <= 4 base via Shaked-Monderer's block lemma and Schur complements (Thm 3.1, pp. 4-5)
Schur complement on a negative first row preserves ordering, s_ik - s_ij >= 0 (Thm 3.5, p. 6)
positive-index relaxed ordering with the same induction (Thm 3.9, pp. 6-8)
orbit cone under positive diagonal scaling and permutation contained in SPN (Cor. 4.2, p. 9)
LP feasibility for diagonal scaling and topological sort of a comparison digraph for permutations (Props. 4.7-4.8, pp. 10-11)

counterexamples: 5-cycle SPN matrix outside the orbit, vv^T with two negative entries, and a 6x6 matrix with threshold sign graphs whose Schur complement is the Horn matrix (Ex. 4.4, Prop. 4.6, Ex. 6.2, pp. 9-15)
alternative proof of convex-objective exactness by a bordered matrix and Finsler's lemma (Prop. 5.4, p. 12)
positioning: Builds on Diananda, Shaked-Monderer and Gokmen-Yildirim; prior exactness results re-proved through Observation 5.2 to show it unifies them; relation to the perfect-graph result stated precisely (threshold graphs a strict subset, but no diagonal conditions) (pp. 1-4, 12, 15).
writing: Main theorem in the introduction with forward pointer; one figure for the relaxed ordering; frank remark that the general framework is hard to check; ends on a comparison with known results instead of a conclusions section (pp. 1, 5, 7, 15).
limits_future: Orbit cone strictly inside SPN for n >= 4; threshold sign graphs not sufficient; scaling and permutation tests separate while the full group is larger; no explicit future-work section (pp. 10-15).

method_links.note: establishes when the tractable DNN/SPN relaxation of a nonconvex QP certifies the exact value, closing a question from his own relaxation work
step 6: the cone-theoretic step done with mathematicians Blekherman and Dunbar and former student Kocuk (Heuristic 8)
each positive result bounded by an explicit example (orbit not all of SPN; sign-graph condition not sufficient)

transferable: Prove copositive-implies-SPN by an induction framework with three checkable closure conditions (one-sign row, deletion, Schur complement) (pp. 4-6).
If a matrix class is invariant under adding multiples of the all-ones matrix, a cone-equality result on the class gives exactness of the StQP relaxation for every objective in it (pp. 11-12).
Check orbit membership under scaling by LP feasibility and under permutation by topological sorting (pp. 10-11).
Show a sufficient condition is not necessary by a matrix with the same sign pattern whose Schur complement is a known counterexample (pp. 14-15).
Re-prove known results with the new lens before stating new ones (p. 12).
coauthors: Grigoriy Blekherman, Alex Dunbar, Burak Kocuk

quotes.text: The hypotheses on classes of matrices in Condition (3.1.III) is recursively defined. In particular, it is difficult to check that a class A satisfies these hypotheses.
Our results, on the other hand, provide conditions under which copositivity implies the existence of an SPN decomposition which apply when the sign graphs are threshold.
